headline: Trump rallies for Hinson today. She says she'll push back.
summary: Trump rallies in Sioux City today for Ashley Hinson, Iowa's Republican nominee for Senate. She launched as his "top ally"; now she calls herself "Iowa's best bipartisan fighter" and has broken with him on beef imports, the Iran war and Russian diesel. Iowa has lost factory jobs and farm profit since he came back. She needs his votes.

cover_question.q: Why take his help and push back?

cover_answer: His loyalists have to show up for her. So she takes both.
table_question: Can you take someone's help and still tell them they're wrong?

5-7.script: Ashley wants a job making laws for the whole country, and Iowa votes on it soon. The President is flying to Iowa today to tell a big crowd to pick her. She says she'll be on his team but tell him when he's wrong, like a friend who still says no to you. Nobody is in trouble; the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A job, a crowd, and a friend who still says no.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them a job, a crowd and a friend who still says no, which is the whole story at this age. The tariffs, the war and the polling stay out. Expect "is he her boss?" No. She wants his voters, and she can still say no to him. Both are true.

8-12.script: Ashley Hinson wants Iowa's Senate seat. Trump is unpopular there: factories closed, farms earned less since he came back. But his loyal voters turn out, so he's rallying for her in Sioux City today. She takes his help and pushes back on beef, the war and Russia. A captain who plays with the star but calls his fouls.
8-12.why: His voters turn out, so she takes him and calls his fouls.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether people apply rules evenly, so the script runs the chain: Trump is unpopular in Iowa, his voters still turn out, so she takes his rally and pushes back where it costs Iowa. The captain calling fouls is the mechanism. Expect "is she being fake?" Her opponent says so. AP has three.

13-17.script: Why take his help and push back? Hinson launched as Trump's "top ally" and now runs as "Iowa's best bipartisan fighter": she keeps his voters and wins one in ten who disapprove of him. Second: she stayed with him on the war vote two Iowa colleagues broke on. Balance, or having it both ways?
13-17.why: Ally, then fighter, then the vote she didn't break on.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: she broke with Trump three times on record, and stayed with him on the war vote her colleagues broke on. The script asks where balance ends and having it both ways begins; they test whether you argue honestly. Expect "so is she a rubber stamp?" Her opponent says yes. Record: sometimes.

5-7.q: Why is the President coming to Iowa?
5-7.a: To ask people to vote for Ashley. He visits lots of states before an election.

8-12.q: Why don't people in Iowa like Trump now?
8-12.a: Factory jobs, clinics and farm profits shrank since he came back, AP says.
No to him on beef, the war and Russian diesel; his side on the rest.

13-17.q: Why take his help and push back?
13-17.a: She needs his loyalists to turn out, and a tenth of his critics are in play.

13-17.q: Is that honest or having it both ways?
13-17.a: Rubber stamp, her opponent says. Three breaks, one vote she didn't. You decide.
